heroLead: Vanderbilt sits up in Otsego County, right in the thick of the Antrim Shale boom that reshaped mineral ownership across northern Michigan.
intro: Otsego County was one of the counties that got hammered with Antrim development in the late 1980s and through the '90s, and Vanderbilt saw its share of it. If you own minerals here, there's a decent chance your family's interest has been generating a royalty check for twenty, thirty, even close to forty years now, quietly stepping down in size as the well ages. A lot of owners never revisit what that interest is worth until they need the cash or an estate forces the issue.
We buy mineral and royalty interests around Vanderbilt and the rest of Otsego County. Straight numbers, pulled from your actual production, no mailbox pressure tactics.

sections.heading: Otsego County's Antrim History
paragraphs: Otsego County is about as core-Antrim as it gets in Michigan. The play here is shallow Devonian black shale gas, biogenic in origin, drilled aggressively during the boom because the shallow depths made it cheap to develop compared to conventional plays elsewhere in the state. Density was high — a lot of 40 and 80-acre spacing units went in around Vanderbilt and the surrounding townships, which is part of why so many local families ended up with a mineral interest of some kind, even a small fractional one.

Nearly four decades on, most of that original wave of wells is deep into decline. The steep early-life drop is long over; what's left is the long low tail that Antrim wells are known for, still paying but at a fraction of peak.

sections.heading: The Niagaran Reef Trend Runs Through This Area Too
paragraphs: Otsego County isn't purely an Antrim story. The Niagaran pinnacle reef trend — an ancient reef system buried deep in the Michigan Basin — runs through a band of northern Michigan counties including parts of Otsego, and reef wells target oil and associated gas at much greater depth than the shallow Antrim gas. If your family's ownership includes older leases from before the Antrim boom, there's a chance some of that paper traces back to reef exploration rather than Antrim development, and that changes how we'd look at your interest.
This is exactly why we ask for your lease and division order before quoting anything — the depth and formation named in that paperwork tells us which play we're actually pricing.

sections.heading: Small Legacy Interests Are the Norm Here, Not the Exception
paragraphs: Because Antrim spacing units were small and drilling was so widespread through this county, a lot of Vanderbilt-area families ended up owning fractional interests measured in tiny percentages — 1/16th, 1/64th, sometimes smaller — after land got divided across generations of heirs. That's normal, and it doesn't mean the interest isn't worth pursuing. It just means the total value on any one piece is modest, and we're upfront about that going in rather than dressing up a small number to get a signature.

If your ownership runs through an estate that was never formally settled, Otsego County's probate court and register of deeds are where that gets straightened out. We can point you toward what's typically needed.

faqs.question: How old are most of the wells around Vanderbilt?
faqs.answer: Most Otsego County Antrim wells were drilled in the late 1980s through the '90s, so many are approaching or past thirty years of production and sitting on the long flat tail of their decline curve.

faqs.question: Could my interest be tied to something other than Antrim gas?
faqs.answer: Possibly. The Niagaran reef trend runs through parts of Otsego County, and older leases sometimes target deeper formations. We check your actual lease and division order before assuming.

faqs.question: My interest is a tiny fraction of a percent. Is it worth selling?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, yes, particularly if it's tied to an active well. We'll give you an honest read rather than telling you what you want to hear.
